procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Tripura at Agartala
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 09.04.2015 of the High Court of Tripura at Agartala in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 189 of 2011 and 109 of 2011 and Writ Petition (Civil) No. 124 of 2012.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Tripura at Agartala issued a Judgment and Order dated 09.04.2015 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 189 of 2011, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 109 of 2011, and Writ Petition (Civil) No. 124 of 2012.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via Special Leave Petitions (SLP(C) Nos. 19765-19767 of 2015). The Supreme Court noted the questions involved required a hearing by a bench as per Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India and ordered the files to be placed before the Chief Justice of India for appropriate bench constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the case should be heard by a Constitution Bench as per the constitutional mandate under Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India.

facts: The case involved petitioners who pleaded for a re-examination of the Supreme Court's previous decision in the *Nagaraj* case.
Specifically, they argued that the 'test of backwardness' should not be applied to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes (SC/ST).
Questions were also raised regarding the application of the 'creamy layer' principle to SC/ST communities notified under Articles 341 and 342 of the Constitution.
law: Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India mandates that any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution must be heard by a bench of at least five judges (a Constitution Bench).
application: The Court considered the nature of the legal questions raised in the case.

It determined that the pleas to reconsider a previous landmark judgment (*Nagaraj*) and to interpret constitutional provisions related to reservations (Articles 16(4), 16(4A), and 16(4B)) constituted substantial questions of constitutional law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, having regard to the substantial constitutional questions involved, the case was required to be heard by a Constitution Bench as per the mandate of Article 145(3). It therefore ordered the matter to be placed before the Chief Justice of India to constitute the appropriate bench.

issue.issue_text: Whether interim relief should be granted at this stage.

facts: The counsel for the parties pressed the court to grant interim relief.
law: Under Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India, any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution must be heard by a bench of at least five judges (a Constitution Bench).
application: The court first determined that the questions involved in the case required it to be heard by a Constitution Bench as per the constitutional mandate.
Given this referral, the court was of the view that the question of whether to grant interim relief should also be considered by the Constitution Bench, not the current bench.
reasoning.conclusion: The court rejected the request for interim relief at this stage, deciding that the matter should be considered by the Constitution Bench that will hear the main case. The court allowed the parties to mention the urgency of the matter to the Chief Justice of India for the constitution of the appropriate bench.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the case should be heard by a Constitution Bench as per the constitutional mandate under Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India.
Whether interim relief should be granted at this stage.
appellant_arguments: The learned counsel pressed for interim relief to be granted.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A case involving a substantial question of law regarding the interpretation of the Constitution must be heard by a Constitution Bench as mandated by Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India.
obiter: The consideration of interim relief in a case that is to be heard by a Constitution Bench should also be deferred to that Bench.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court determined that the questions involved in the case were significant enough to require a hearing by a Constitution Bench, as mandated by Article 145(3) of the Constitution. Consequently, the court also held that the decision on whether to grant interim relief should be deferred and considered by that same Constitution Bench.
legal_tests_applied: Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India, which requires a case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution to be heard by a Bench of at least five judges.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's request for interim relief was denied because the court was of the view that 'even that stage needs to be considered by the Constitution Bench.'
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the position that the case should be heard by a larger bench, stating, 'Having regard to the questions involved in this case, we are of the opinion that this is a case to be heard by a Bench as per the constitutional mandate under Article 145(3) of the Constitution of India.'
The court effectively sided with the respondent's position on interim relief by deferring the decision, reasoning that the Constitution Bench should be the one to consider it.
